summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity is legal; it was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. No traveller-facing restrictions are in force: there are no bathroom or facilities laws, no documented inspection of gender markers at the border, and no recorded pattern of police targeting trans visitors.

Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery, and no nonbinary recognition is available. A visitor whose passport carries a marker inconsistent with presentation has no documented record of friction at Panamanian entry points, though the surgery requirement shapes which documents residents are able to obtain in the first place.

No statute prohibits discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. The National Assembly blocked an amendment to the general anti-discrimination law in 2024, on the stated basis that existing provisions cover such grounds implicitly, and a 2015 bill to bar discrimination on sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds has not advanced. No acts are formally recognised as hate crimes, so violence against a trans visitor would not be charged or recorded under a hate-crime regime.

Partner recognition is restricted. Article 40 of the Code of Private International Law, approved 8 May 2014, states that same-sex marriages are strictly prohibited and that foreign same-sex marriages will not be recognised, which bears directly on a visitor travelling with a same-sex spouse. The Supreme Court ruled on 27 March 2023, after a seven-year delay, that there is no positive right to same-sex marriage under the constitution. A constitutional amendment defining marriage as between a man and a woman was approved by the National Assembly on 29 October 2019 but withdrawn before referendum following public protests.

Litigation over marriage ran from 2017, when two suits were combined after oral arguments, through a draft ruling by Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega in October 2017 that the family code's same-sex marriage bars were not unconstitutional while leaving the legislature to consider civil unions; the justice withdrew that draft in February 2018. The government signalled it would comply with the Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision of 9 January 2018, but no implementing legislation followed.

At the 2025 UN Universal Periodic Review multiple states urged Panama to adopt explicit anti-discrimination protections, reform gender recognition and strengthen safeguards against violence. Those recommendations remain unimplemented and legal reform is stalled, leaving Panama behind much of the region.
tangentialFactors:
Public opinion constrains reform. Only 12% of Panamanians approve of same-sex marriage, ranking Panama 18th of 22 in the AmericasBarometer 2023, and a 2017 public survey found 78% opposed. The Roman Catholic Church defeated a 2004 civil-union proposal, condemned the 2018 Inter-American Court advisory opinion, and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition to the 2017 marriage litigation; one deputy labelled that opinion "a danger to the human race".

Article 39 of the Constitution, which bars associations contrary to moral or legal order, has been used to refuse registration of gay organisations. The first gay group, founded in 1996, obtained legal recognition only in 2005 after a three-year battle.

Cultural context varies sharply by place. In the Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing third-gender community, the Omeggid, is described as accepted as completely normal, with matriarchal figures elevating the status of women, per a 2018 feature.

Adjacent health rules: gay and bisexual men are barred from donating blood, with an indefinite deferral, and conversion therapy is not banned.
localsOnly:
Residents face the surgery requirement for legal gender recognition, with no nonbinary option, and have no statutory protection against discrimination in employment or housing.

Intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited or regulated, and no law bans conversion therapy.

Registration of LGBT organisations remains exposed to Article 39 of the Constitution, and the 2015 anti-discrimination bill and the 2024 amendment to the general anti-discrimination law have both failed in the National Assembly.

Residents in same-sex marriages contracted abroad have no route to recognition under Article 40 of the Code of Private International Law, and the 2023 Supreme Court ruling forecloses a constitutional right to same-sex marriage absent new legislation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records either friction or its absence at Panamanian border points for trans travellers presenting documents inconsistent with their appearance; the assessment rests on the absence of any recorded incident rather than on an affirmative official statement or published entry guidance.

Whether the Inter-American Court decision of 9 January 2018 has been implemented through any pending bill is unresolved here; the sources record the government's signal of compliance and the subsequent 2023 Supreme Court ruling, but no legislative outcome.

Outcomes for trans victims of violence, including police handling of complaints, are not sourced. The non-recognition of hate crimes is established, but no case data accompanies it.
